question_text: A RAG application covers millions of documents across three distinct domains: legal, technical, and financial. The team wants to partition the vector space by domain for improved retrieval precision. Which approach is most suitable?

options.text: A single Amazon OpenSearch index with all vectors and a metadata filter at query time
Amazon OpenSearch with the Neural plugin, using separate indices per domain (multi-index approach)
Amazon DynamoDB with a composite key that encodes the domain
A single Aurora pgvector table with a domain column

explanation: Skills 1.4.1 and 1.4.3 describe multi-index approaches for specialised domains using Amazon OpenSearch Service with the Neural plugin for Bedrock integration and topic-based segmentation. Separate indices give independent ANN graphs per domain, providing both search precision and performance at scale. A single mixed index reduces precision. DynamoDB lacks native vector search. A single pgvector table with a WHERE clause can work at smaller scale but not hundreds-of-millions of vectors.
source_topic: OpenSearch multi-index, vector database, RAG

question_text: A RAG system should prefer the most recently published documents when vector similarity scores are similar. How should this be implemented?

options.text: Embed the document creation date as part of the text before generating embeddings
Store document timestamps as S3 object metadata and incorporate a recency score into the hybrid scoring function
Delete older documents from the vector store regularly to enforce recency by elimination
Use a smaller embedding dimension for newer documents so they cluster separately

explanation: Skill 1.4.2 describes S3 object metadata for document timestamps and custom attributes to develop metadata frameworks that improve search precision. Combining cosine similarity with a recency decay factor in a hybrid scorer implements date-preference cleanly. Embedding dates in text adds noise to semantic vectors. Deleting old documents destroys institutional knowledge. Varying embedding dimensions breaks the vector space — dimensions must be consistent.
source_topic: Vector store metadata, S3 object metadata, hybrid scoring

question_text: An OpenSearch cluster storing 500 million 1536-dimension embeddings is experiencing increasing query latency. Which TWO changes most directly improve performance?

options.text: Increase the number of primary shards to distribute the index across more nodes
Switch from exact k-NN to approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) with HNSW algorithm
Add read replica shards to improve availability
Reduce vector dimensions by switching to a smaller embedding model
Enable cross-cluster replication to a different region

explanation: Skill 1.4.3 cites OpenSearch sharding strategies and high-performance vector database architectures. (A) More primary shards distribute the index, reducing per-shard size and enabling search parallelism. (B) ANN/HNSW runs in O(log n) vs exact k-NN's O(n) — a massive improvement at 500M vectors. Read replicas (C) improve read throughput/availability but don't reduce per-query latency. Changing embedding dimensions (D) would degrade retrieval quality. Cross-cluster replication (E) is for disaster recovery, not latency.
source_topic: OpenSearch sharding, HNSW, ANN search

question_text: A company's internal wiki is continuously edited by hundreds of employees. The RAG system must reflect edits within 15 minutes. Which approach meets this SLA?

options.text: Run a nightly batch job that re-indexes all documents from scratch
Implement event-driven change detection that triggers incremental re-embedding and index updates within minutes of each edit
Require employees to manually trigger re-indexing after each edit
Increase the context window size so the FM can work with stale data

explanation: Skill 1.4.5 describes real-time change detection systems, automated synchronisation workflows, and incremental update mechanisms. A nightly batch job produces up to 24-hour staleness — violating the 15-minute SLA. Manual triggers are unreliable and scale poorly. Context window size is irrelevant to index freshness.
source_topic: Vector store synchronisation, incremental updates, event-driven

question_text: A startup is building a RAG app with up to 5 million document chunks. Their team has deep PostgreSQL expertise and can tolerate up to 500 ms retrieval latency. Which vector store is the BEST fit?

options.text: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector engine
Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension
Amazon DynamoDB with a custom embedding attribute
Amazon S3 with a sequential Python similarity scan

explanation: Skill 1.5.3 lists Amazon Aurora with pgvector as a valid vector search solution. At 5M chunks, 500 ms tolerance, and existing PostgreSQL expertise, Aurora pgvector is the best fit — familiar operational model, ACID guarantees, and solid ANN performance within these scale parameters. OpenSearch Serverless excels at hundreds of millions of vectors with sub-100ms SLAs. DynamoDB has no native vector search. An S3 linear scan is O(n) — completely infeasible at 5M vectors.
source_topic: Aurora pgvector, OpenSearch Serverless, vector store selection

topic: Knowledge Base integration with document systems
question_text: A company wants to connect their SharePoint document repository to Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases so employees can query it via a GenAI assistant. What is the correct integration approach?

options.text: Manually export SharePoint documents to S3 daily using a scheduled Lambda
Use an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base data source connector (e.g., SharePoint connector) for automated ingestion
Train a fine-tuned model on SharePoint content to embed knowledge directly in weights
Use Amazon Kendra SharePoint connector instead of Bedrock

explanation: Skill 1.4.4 describes using AWS services to create integration components that connect resources (document management systems, knowledge bases, internal wikis). Bedrock Knowledge Bases provides native data source connectors for SharePoint, Confluence, S3, and other repositories — automating ingestion and synchronisation. Manual daily Lambda exports create staleness. Fine-tuning embeds knowledge in weights with no ability to update or query source documents. Kendra is being closed to new customers (July 2026).
source_topic: Bedrock Knowledge Bases connectors, SharePoint integration

topic: Vector store backends for Bedrock KB
question_text: A team wants to use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases but needs to keep their vectors in their existing Amazon OpenSearch Service domain for operational reasons. Is this possible?

options.text: No — Bedrock Knowledge Bases only supports its own fully managed vector store
Yes — configure the Knowledge Base to use an existing OpenSearch Service domain or OpenSearch Serverless collection as the backing store
Yes — but only if you first migrate from OpenSearch to Amazon MemoryDB
No — only Amazon DynamoDB is supported as an external vector store

explanation: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases supports multiple backing vector stores: Amazon OpenSearch Service, OpenSearch Serverless, Amazon Aurora, Amazon RDS, MongoDB Atlas, Pinecone, and Redis Enterprise Cloud. Teams can bring their existing OpenSearch domain while still using Bedrock's managed ingestion and retrieval APIs. Only the fully managed option (Amazon OpenSearch Serverless) requires no external infra; all others let you bring your own.
source_topic: Bedrock Knowledge Bases, vector store backends

topic: S3 Vectors for infrequent large-scale search
question_text: An earth-observation company stores embeddings for 500 million satellite images. Analysts run similarity searches only a few times per week. The priority is minimum cost with no infrastructure to manage. Which vector store is the best fit?

options.text: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector engine
Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector
Amazon S3 Vectors — a serverless S3 vector bucket with pay-per-query pricing
Amazon DynamoDB with a custom Lambda similarity scan

explanation: Amazon S3 Vectors is purpose-built for cost-optimised, large-scale, infrequently queried vector workloads (Skill 1.4.1, vector store architectures). It is truly serverless — no always-on compute — and charges only for storage and actual queries, approximately 90% cheaper than OpenSearch for sparse access patterns. OpenSearch Serverless charges minimum OCUs even when idle. Aurora/pgvector requires a provisioned DB instance with hourly charges. DynamoDB has no native vector search — scanning 500M records via Lambda would be impractically slow and expensive.
source_topic: Amazon S3 Vectors, cost-optimised vector storage

question_text: A company wants their FM assistant to always answer based on the latest internal HR policies, which are updated several times a year. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Fine-tune the FM on the HR policy documents each time they are updated
Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases (RAG) — index the current policy documents and retrieve relevant sections at query time
Increase the FM context window so it can hold all policies in every prompt
Pre-train the FM from scratch on HR data

explanation: RAG via Bedrock Knowledge Bases (Skill 1.4) is the correct pattern for frequently-updated proprietary documents. Re-ingesting updated S3 documents takes minutes. Fine-tuning (A) bakes knowledge into weights — expensive, slow, and must be fully re-run on every document change. Stuffing all policies into every prompt (C) rapidly exceeds context windows for large corpora and wastes tokens on every call. Pre-training from scratch (D) is the most expensive option and is out-of-scope for application developers.
source_topic: Bedrock Knowledge Bases, RAG vs fine-tuning

topic: Amazon MemoryDB as in-memory vector store
question_text: A retail company is building a real-time product recommendation assistant that requires sub-10 ms vector similarity search with durable storage. Which AWS-native vector store option is BEST suited?

options.text: Amazon MemoryDB with vector search enabled
Amazon S3 with a Lambda function performing brute-force cosine similarity
Amazon RDS MySQL with a BLOB column storing raw embeddings
Amazon SQS as a vector storage layer

explanation: Amazon MemoryDB is a durable, in-memory database with native vector search, purpose-built for workloads that need single-digit millisecond latency at scale. S3 with Lambda brute-force is slow and unscalable for real-time use. RDS MySQL with BLOB has no vector indexing capability. SQS is a message queue — not a data store — and has no vector search.
source_topic: Amazon MemoryDB vector search, low-latency retrieval

question_text: A B2B SaaS company hosts a single Bedrock Knowledge Base for multiple enterprise customers, each of whom must only receive answers derived from their own documents. Which approach CORRECTLY enforces tenant isolation at retrieval time?

options.text: Tag every document chunk with a tenant_id metadata attribute and apply a metadata filter on every retrieval request
Provision a separate knowledge base (and vector index) for each tenant
Rely on the model's context window to naturally separate tenant documents
Use a higher temperature value to mix tenant results less frequently
Return all results and let the application post-filter by tenant after retrieval

explanation: Tenant-level metadata filtering (option A) is an efficient single-index approach: each chunk is tagged with a tenant identifier and only matching chunks are returned. Separate knowledge bases per tenant (option B) provide full physical isolation. The model's context window provides no isolation (C). Temperature affects generation randomness, not retrieval isolation (D). Post-filtering after retrieval (E) is insecure because documents from other tenants could still be passed to the model before being filtered.
source_topic: Multi-tenant RAG, metadata filtering, knowledge base isolation

question_text: A knowledge graph application stores entities (products, customers, suppliers) and their relationships. The team wants to augment retrieval by combining graph traversal with vector similarity search — for example finding products similar to a description AND connected to a supplier in a specific region. Which AWS service supports this graph+vector hybrid approach?

options.text: Amazon Neptune Analytics — supports vector similarity search alongside graph analytics on the same dataset
Amazon DynamoDB — a key-value store with no graph or vector search
Amazon Redshift — a columnar warehouse without graph traversal
Amazon Kinesis — a streaming service with no storage or query capability

explanation: Amazon Neptune Analytics adds vector search to Neptune's graph engine, enabling queries that traverse relationships (graph) and simultaneously find semantically similar nodes (vector). This is uniquely suited to knowledge graph RAG use cases. DynamoDB is a key-value store. Redshift is a columnar warehouse. Kinesis is a streaming ingest service.
source_topic: Neptune Analytics, graph vector search, knowledge graph RAG

topic: S3 Vectors for infrequent large-scale search
question_text: A company has 500 million document embeddings that are queried infrequently (monthly batch jobs). They need the lowest possible storage cost for these vectors. Which vector store is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Amazon MemoryDB for Redis
Amazon OpenSearch Service (provisioned)
Amazon S3 Vectors
Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector

explanation: Amazon S3 Vectors is the lowest-cost vector storage option on AWS, designed for large, cold datasets where queries are infrequent. It leverages S3's economics for bulk storage. MemoryDB is in-memory and optimised for ultra-low latency (and is most expensive at scale). OpenSearch provisioned clusters have ongoing compute costs regardless of query frequency. Aurora pgvector is suited for small/medium relational datasets, not 500M vectors at minimal cost.
source_topic: S3 Vectors for cold, large-scale vector storage

topic: OpenSearch HNSW vs IVF algorithm selection
question_text: A search team is configuring OpenSearch for a RAG system with 50 million embeddings. They prioritise low query latency and high recall over memory efficiency. Which approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) algorithm should they choose?

options.text: IVF (Inverted File Index) — optimised for minimal memory use
HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) — optimised for low latency and high recall
BM25 — keyword-based sparse retrieval
k-Means clustering with centroid lookup

explanation: HNSW is the recommended ANN algorithm when low latency and high recall are the primary goals. It uses a multi-layer graph structure that enables fast, accurate approximate search at the cost of higher memory usage. IVF uses an inverted file structure that is more memory-efficient but trades some recall and latency. BM25 is a keyword/sparse retrieval algorithm, not an ANN algorithm. k-Means centroid lookup is not a standard OpenSearch algorithm.
source_topic: OpenSearch HNSW vs IVF for vector search

topic: OpenSearch HNSW vs IVF algorithm selection
question_text: A platform engineer is configuring OpenSearch vector search for a dataset of 2 billion embeddings. Memory is constrained and they can tolerate slightly lower recall in exchange for significant memory savings. Which ANN algorithm is BEST suited?

options.text: HNSW — high recall but memory-intensive
IVF (Inverted File) — lower memory with tunable recall-speed trade-off
Exact nearest-neighbour — highest accuracy but slowest
Random projection — fast but lowest recall

explanation: IVF is designed for very large datasets where memory savings are important. It partitions the vector space into clusters (inverted file lists) and only searches within the nearest clusters at query time. This reduces memory compared to HNSW and allows the recall/speed trade-off to be tuned via the nprobe parameter. HNSW would require significantly more RAM for 2B vectors. Exact NN becomes impractically slow at this scale.
source_topic: IVF for memory-constrained large vector datasets

question_text: A team wants OpenSearch to accept raw text queries and automatically generate embeddings internally using Amazon Bedrock embedding models — without writing any client-side embedding code. Which OpenSearch feature enables this?

options.text: OpenSearch k-NN plugin with manual vector submission
OpenSearch Neural Plugin with a Bedrock ML connector
Bedrock Knowledge Base with OpenSearch Serverless backing store
Amazon Comprehend topic modelling integrated with OpenSearch

explanation: The OpenSearch Neural Plugin allows OpenSearch to call external embedding models (via ML connectors, including Bedrock) as part of ingest and search pipelines. This means raw text goes in, OpenSearch generates the embedding internally, and returns results — no client-side embedding code needed. The k-NN plugin requires the client to pre-compute and submit vectors. Bedrock Knowledge Bases manage the full pipeline but the client doesn't control OpenSearch internals. Comprehend does NLP, not embedding generation.
source_topic: OpenSearch Neural Plugin for text-in/vector-out

question_text: A multi-tenant SaaS company stores all customer documents in a single Bedrock Knowledge Base. They need to ensure that when a user from Company A queries the knowledge base, only Company A's documents are retrieved. What is the CORRECT mechanism for this in Bedrock Knowledge Bases?

options.text: Create a separate Knowledge Base per tenant
Use IAM conditions to restrict Bedrock invocations by tenant
Attach a metadata.json file to each document with a tenant_id attribute, then apply metadata filters at query time
Use Bedrock Guardrails denied topics to restrict cross-tenant content

explanation: Bedrock Knowledge Bases support metadata.json files that attach key-value attributes (like tenant_id) to document chunks. At query time, you apply a metadata filter (e.g., tenant_id = 'company-a') to restrict retrieval to only the matching chunks. This enables multi-tenant isolation within a single knowledge base. Separate KBs per tenant (A) works but is operationally expensive at scale. IAM conditions control API access, not which documents are retrieved. Guardrails denied topics filter generated content, not retrieval.
source_topic: metadata.json for multi-tenant Knowledge Base filtering

question_text: A real-time recommender system needs to perform vector similarity search with sub-millisecond latency on a dataset of 10 million embeddings. Cost is secondary to latency. Which AWS vector store is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Amazon S3 Vectors
Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector
Amazon MemoryDB
Amazon OpenSearch Serverless

explanation: Amazon MemoryDB is a durable, in-memory database with native vector search capabilities, optimised for ultra-low latency (sub-millisecond) queries at high throughput. All data resides in memory, which is what enables sub-millisecond performance. S3 Vectors is lowest cost but has disk-based latency. Aurora pgvector is disk-based relational storage with moderate vector search latency. OpenSearch Serverless offers good latency but not sub-millisecond for in-memory access patterns.
source_topic: MemoryDB for ultra-low-latency vector search

topic: DynamoDB for session state vs vector search
question_text: A developer is designing a conversational AI application and needs to store conversation history (session state) that is tied to a user session ID and can be automatically deleted after 24 hours of inactivity. Which AWS service is MOST appropriate for this requirement?

options.text: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless
Amazon S3 with lifecycle rules
Amazon DynamoDB with TTL (Time-to-Live) attribute
Amazon MemoryDB

explanation: DynamoDB with TTL is the standard pattern for storing session state (conversation history) keyed by session/conversation ID. TTL automatically deletes items after a configurable expiry time — no cron job or Lambda cleanup needed. OpenSearch is a search engine optimised for querying, not key-value session storage. S3 lifecycle rules work for objects but add complexity for per-session expiry. MemoryDB is in-memory and expensive for this use case; TTL management requires more configuration than DynamoDB TTL.
source_topic: DynamoDB TTL for session state and chat history

topic: Vector store backends for Bedrock KB
question_text: A team is selecting a vector store backend for a new Bedrock Knowledge Base. They already run an Aurora PostgreSQL cluster and want to add vector search capability with minimal new infrastructure. Which backing store is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless
Amazon Neptune Analytics
Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector extension
Amazon S3 Vectors

explanation: If the team already runs Aurora PostgreSQL, enabling the pgvector extension adds vector similarity search to the existing database with minimal new infrastructure — no new service to provision. OpenSearch Serverless would require a new cluster. Neptune Analytics is for graph + vector workloads. S3 Vectors is cheapest for cold/infrequent workloads, not active transactional databases.
source_topic: Aurora pgvector for existing PostgreSQL deployments

question_text: An OpenSearch cluster serving a RAG system is experiencing high query latency as the vector index grows to 200 million embeddings. The cluster currently has 1 primary shard. What is the BEST remediation?

options.text: Increase the ef_search parameter to improve recall
Switch from HNSW to exact nearest-neighbour search
Redistribute the index across multiple shards to parallelise search
Add more replica shards without changing the number of primary shards

explanation: A single primary shard is the bottleneck for a 200M-vector index because all queries hit that single shard sequentially. Distributing the index across multiple primary shards allows the query to fan out and execute in parallel across nodes, reducing latency. Increasing ef_search improves recall accuracy but increases latency. Exact NN would be even slower. Adding replica shards improves read throughput and availability but doesn't help if a single primary shard is the bottleneck.
source_topic: OpenSearch sharding strategy for large vector indices

question_text: A company uses DynamoDB as its primary data store for product catalogue items. When a product is updated, the corresponding vector embedding in an OpenSearch index must be updated within seconds. Which pattern achieves this with the LEAST operational complexity?

options.text: Run a nightly Glue ETL job to re-embed and re-index all products
Use DynamoDB Streams to trigger a Lambda function that re-embeds and updates the OpenSearch index
Manually update OpenSearch whenever a product is changed via the admin console
Use Amazon EventBridge scheduled rules to poll DynamoDB for changes every 5 minutes

explanation: DynamoDB Streams captures item-level changes in real time and can trigger a Lambda function for each change. The Lambda re-embeds the updated product description and updates the OpenSearch index, achieving near-real-time sync. Nightly Glue jobs introduce up to 24 hours of staleness. Manual console updates are not scalable. EventBridge scheduled polling every 5 minutes introduces unnecessary delay and complexity.
source_topic: DynamoDB Streams → Lambda → OpenSearch real-time sync

question_text: A legal tech company wants to build a RAG system that not only retrieves documents by semantic similarity but also traverses relationships between legal entities, cases, and citations (graph relationships). Which vector store backing for Bedrock Knowledge Bases BEST supports this hybrid graph + vector search requirement?

options.text: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless
Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector
Amazon Neptune Analytics
Amazon S3 Vectors

explanation: Amazon Neptune Analytics supports both graph traversal (relationships between entities) and vector similarity search — making it the only AWS-native backing store that can handle the hybrid graph + vector requirement. OpenSearch and Aurora pgvector support vector search but not native graph traversal. S3 Vectors is purely a bulk vector store with no graph capabilities.
source_topic: Neptune Analytics for graph + vector hybrid RAG

topic: Avoid cluster management with OpenSearch Serverless
question_text: A startup team wants to add vector search to their RAG pipeline using Amazon OpenSearch but does not want to manage shard counts, replica configuration, or cluster sizing. Which OpenSearch option minimises operational overhead?

options.text: Amazon OpenSearch Service (provisioned) with auto-scaling enabled
Amazon OpenSearch Serverless
OpenSearch on Amazon EC2 (self-managed)
Elasticsearch on Amazon EKS

explanation: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless automatically handles capacity, sharding, and scaling without requiring the team to manage cluster configurations. You pay per OCU (OpenSearch Compute Unit) consumed, not for idle cluster capacity. Provisioned OpenSearch still requires configuring shards, instance types, and replica counts. Self-managed options on EC2 or EKS have the highest operational overhead.
source_topic: OpenSearch Serverless for no-ops vector search
